newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Hostages said taken by rebels in south Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Hostages said taken by rebels in south Philippines.

text.p: At least six people died in renewed fighting in the southern Philippines on Thursday, and the army accused Moslem rebels of seizing dozens of bus passengers to stop advancing soldiers.

Defence Secretary Renato de Villa said troopers had rescued several of the hostages. But an army spokesman contradicted the report, saying they escaped at the height of the fighting on a country road near Cotabato city.
A spokesman for the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) denied the guerrillas took any hostage at all.

"What happened was that several buses were passing by and we stopped them and asked them not to proceed because they would be in the line of fire between our troops and the government," MILF political officer Al Mujaheed told Reuters by telephone.
He said the guerrillas had withdrawn from the area, leaving the passengers behind.
Mujaheed denied a police report that the rebels had shot dead two passengers, including a man carrying a police identification card, before retreating to the forests.

Brigadier-General Ronnie Benedicto, head of the southern military command, said four guerrillas and two soldiers were killed in a gun battle that broke out on a road in Kabacan town after rebels stopped passenger buses from driving through their area.
Benedicto said the retreating guerrillas took about 60 passengers hostage. Manila radio stations, quoting other army sources, said the number topped 100.
Private radio station DZMM, quoting police, said about 40 passengers later escaped from the rebels during the battle with the soldiers.
There was no immediate official report on the number of passengers involved in the incident.

More than 30,000 villagers have fled their homes and least 45 people, mostly rebels, have been killed in more than a week of fighting that began after MILF rebels briefly took over a state-owned oil and gas exploration site on Mindanao island.
The military has sent in six MG-520 rocket-firing helicopters to back up its offensive and has closed a key road link between the cities of Cotabato and Davao.
MILF leaders have said the military offensive could scupper peace talks due to restart this weekend.
The MILF, estimated to have 8,000 armed fighters, is battling for independence for Mindanao, an ancestral Moslem homeland in the predominantly Christian Philippines.
It stayed out of a peace treaty signed late last year by Manila and the mainstream Islamic separatist group, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF).
